prompt: What defines a minimum (minimal) basis set?

choices.text: One basis function for each atomic orbital
Two basis functions for each atomic orbital
choices.why: Two functions per orbital is a double-ζ basis. A minimum basis uses a single function for each atomic orbital on each atom.

choices.text: One basis function for each electron
choices.why: Functions go with orbitals, not electrons: a filled 1s orbital holds two electrons but gets just one function.

choices.text: One basis function for each atom
choices.why: One per atom is far too few; each atom from Li to Ne gets five. A minimum basis has one function for each atomic orbital.

explanation: In a minimum basis set, a single basis function is used for each atomic orbital on each atom in the system. It is the smallest kind of basis set.

prompt: A lithium atom has electrons only in its 1s and 2s orbitals. What does a minimum basis set for lithium add to the 1s and 2s functions?

choices.why: d functions are polarization functions, an extra beyond the minimum basis. For lithium the minimum basis adds p-type functions.
Two functions for one orbital belongs to a double-ζ basis. The minimum basis for lithium adds p-type functions instead.
The section says p-type functions are added for atoms such as lithium, so every atom from Li to Ne gets the same five functions.

explanation: For atoms such as lithium, p-type functions are added to the 1s and 2s functions. So each atom from Li to Ne has five functions in a minimum basis: two s and three p.

prompt: In a minimal STO-nG basis set, to which orbitals does the integer n apply?

choices.why: n isn't limited to the core. In STO-nG every STO, core or valence, is approximated by n Gaussians.
The core orbitals are fitted with n Gaussians too. In STO-nG the same n is used for core and valence orbitals.
n applies to every STO in the basis, on every atom, for both core and valence orbitals.

explanation: In STO-nG, n is the number of Gaussians used to approximate each Slater-type orbital, for both core and valence orbitals. Split-valence names such as 6-31G instead use different numbers for the core and the valence shell.

prompt: How does the section describe the results of calculations with minimal basis sets?

choices.why: No finite basis is exact, and a minimal one is the least flexible. Its results are rough.
It's the reverse: minimal basis sets are fast, but their rough results are insufficient for research-quality publication.
Anions need extra diffuse functions, which a minimal basis lacks. Minimal basis results are rough in general.

explanation: Minimal basis sets typically give rough results that are insufficient for research-quality publication. Larger, extended basis sets are needed for accurate work.

prompt: What is the main advantage of a minimal basis set over larger basis sets?

choices.why: Minimal basis sets are the least accurate; their results are rough. Their advantage is cost.
Anions call for diffuse functions, added to larger basis sets. The minimal basis wins only on cost.
Adjustable orbital sizes come from double-ζ and larger basis sets. A minimal basis is simply much cheaper.

explanation: Minimal basis sets need far fewer calculations than larger basis sets, so they are much cheaper. The price is rough results.

prompt: Which of these basis sets is a minimal basis set?

choices.why: The hyphen in 6-31G marks a split-valence set, in which each valence orbital gets two functions.
3-21G is a split-valence set, like 6-31G: its valence orbitals get two functions each.
6-311G splits each valence orbital into three functions, so it is far from minimal.

explanation: The most common minimal basis sets are of the STO-nG type, such as STO-3G, STO-4G and STO-6G. Names of the form N-MPG, such as 6-31G and 3-21G, are split-valence sets.

prompt: Why is a minimal basis set not flexible enough for accurate results?

choices.text: It has far too many functions on each atom
choices.why: A minimal basis has the fewest functions possible. The problem is that each orbital has only one function.

choices.text: It is built from Gaussians instead of STOs
choices.why: Larger basis sets such as 6-31G are built from Gaussians too. The problem is having only one function for each orbital.

choices.text: It leaves out the core orbitals
choices.why: A minimal basis includes the core orbitals. Its weakness is one fixed function per orbital, where accuracy needs several.

explanation: Accurate results need several functions to represent each atomic orbital. With only one function, of fixed size, an orbital can't adjust to its surroundings in the molecule.

prompt: A double-ζ basis writes the 2s orbital as φ = a_1φ_2s^(STO)(r, ζ_1) + a_2φ_2s^(STO)(r, ζ_2). How do the two STOs in this sum differ?

choices.text: In their shape, s versus p
choices.why: Both terms are 2s STOs, so both are spherical. They differ only in ζ.
Both are 2s functions with the same n. The only difference is the value of ζ.

choices.text: In which nucleus they sit on
choices.why: Both describe the 2s orbital of the same atom. They differ only in ζ, which sets how large each one is.

explanation: The two terms are the same 2s STO except for ζ, which accounts for how large the orbital is. Using two different ζ values gives one smaller and one larger function.

prompt: In the double-ζ orbital φ = a_1φ_2s^(STO)(r, ζ_1) + a_2φ_2s^(STO)(r, ζ_2), what do the constants a_1 and a_2 determine?

choices.why: The size of each STO is set by ζ_1 and ζ_2. The constants a_1 and a_2 weight the two STOs in the sum.

choices.text: The number of nodes in each STO
choices.why: Both terms are 2s STOs, and the a values don't change their shape. They set how much each STO contributes.

choices.text: The number of Gaussians in each STO
choices.why: Gaussians aren't part of this equation, which uses two STOs. a_1 and a_2 set each STO's share of the final orbital.

explanation: a_1 and a_2 determine how much each STO contributes to the final atomic orbital. Mixing a smaller and a larger function in the right proportions gives an orbital of the right size.

prompt: A double-ζ orbital is written φ = a_1φ^(STO)(r, ζ_1) + a_2φ^(STO)(r, ζ_2). Would a_1, a_2, ζ_1 and ζ_2 take the same values for hydrogen and for lithium?

choices.text: No; they vary with the type of atom

choices.why: They aren't universal. The section says hydrogen and lithium orbitals have different a_1, a_2, ζ_1 and ζ_2 values.

choices.text: Yes; both have one valence electron
choices.why: Having one valence electron each doesn't make their orbitals alike: the nuclear charges and orbital sizes differ, and so do the values.

choices.text: No; only a_1 changes between atoms
choices.why: All four values change from atom to atom, the ζ values as well as both a values.

explanation: The values of a_1, a_2, ζ_1 and ζ_2 depend on the type of atom the orbital belongs to. Hydrogen and lithium orbitals have different values.

prompt: A double-ζ basis represents each atomic orbital with two STOs of different size. What does this flexibility let the calculation do?

choices.text: Adjust the size of each orbital
Add an extra node to each orbital
choices.why: Extra nodes come from polarization functions. Two STOs of different size let the orbital's size adjust.
The calculation is still a Hartree–Fock calculation. The double-ζ basis just gives each orbital an adjustable size.

choices.text: Use fewer functions than a minimal one
choices.why: A double-ζ basis has twice as many functions as a minimal one. In exchange, each orbital's size can adjust.

explanation: Mixing a smaller and a larger STO lets the calculation generate atomic orbitals of adjustable size. The valence electron density is then better represented than with one fixed function.

prompt: What trade-off comes with moving from a double-ζ basis to a triple- or quadruple-ζ basis?

choices.why: It's the reverse: more functions per orbital improve accuracy and make the calculations more expensive.

choices.text: Better accuracy at no extra cost
choices.why: More basis functions always mean more calculations. Better accuracy is paid for with higher cost.
Adding functions makes the basis more flexible, so accuracy improves. Only the cost goes up.

explanation: Triple- and quadruple-ζ basis sets use three and four STOs for each orbital instead of two. The typical trade-off applies: better accuracy, but more expensive calculations.

prompt: Have basis sets with more than four basis functions per atomic orbital been built?

choices.text: No; four is the largest possible
choices.why: There's no limit at four. Higher-order sets such as 5Z and 6Z have been constructed.
No finite basis is exact, and higher-order sets such as 5Z and 6Z have been built.
Higher-order sets such as 5Z and 6Z aren't limited to the lightest atoms.

explanation: Beyond quadruple-ζ, higher-order basis sets have been constructed too, such as 5Z and 6Z. The largest basis sets contain dozens to hundreds of functions on each atom.

prompt: Which list orders these basis-set types from fewest to most basis functions per atomic orbital?

choices.why: A minimal basis has one function per orbital, fewer than the two of a double-ζ basis.
Triple-ζ has three functions per orbital, more than the two of double-ζ.
This list runs the wrong way, from most to fewest. A minimal basis has the fewest, one per orbital.

explanation: A minimal basis has one function for each atomic orbital, a double-ζ basis two, a triple-ζ three and a quadruple-ζ four.

prompt: Which of these is one of the types of extended basis sets the section lists?

choices.why: Single-ζ means one function per orbital, which is a minimal basis, not an extended one.
Hydrogenic orbitals aren't on the list. The extended Gaussian sets listed are split-valence, polarized, diffuse and correlation consistent sets.
Plane waves are used in materials calculations, but they aren't Gaussian sets and aren't among the extended types listed.

explanation: The section lists several types of extended basis sets: split-valence, polarized, diffuse and correlation consistent sets. All of them go beyond one function per orbital.

prompt: How many basis functions on each atom can the largest Gaussian basis sets contain?

choices.why: Five is the minimal basis for an atom from Li to Ne. The largest sets have dozens to hundreds of functions per atom.
One per orbital describes a minimal basis, the smallest kind. The largest sets go far beyond it.

choices.text: No more than one per electron
choices.why: The number of functions isn't capped by the number of electrons. The largest sets have dozens to hundreds per atom.

explanation: Today there are hundreds of Gaussian basis sets. The smallest are minimal sets, while the largest contain dozens to hundreds of basis functions on each atom.

prompt: In a split-valence basis-set name of the form N-MPG, such as 6-31G, what does the hyphen indicate?

choices.text: That the valence shell is split

choices.why: The hyphen is part of the name, not a minus sign; 6-31G isn't 6 − 31. It marks a split-valence set.
Polarization functions are marked by an asterisk, as in 6-31G*. The hyphen marks a split-valence set.

choices.text: That the core orbitals are left out
choices.why: The core orbitals are kept: the digit before the hyphen counts the Gaussians for each of them.

explanation: In N-MPG, the hyphen denotes a split-valence set: each valence orbital is described by two functions. N before the hyphen counts the Gaussians for each inner-shell orbital.

prompt: In a split-valence name N-MPG, which letter gives the number of Gaussian functions used for the smaller of the two valence orbitals?

choices.why: P counts the Gaussians for the larger valence orbital, not the smaller one.
N, before the hyphen, counts the Gaussians for each inner-shell orbital.
G isn't a number. It shows that the basis is made of Gaussian functions.

explanation: M counts the Gaussians used to describe the smaller valence orbital and P those for the larger one. In 6-31G, the smaller function uses 3 Gaussians and the larger uses 1.

prompt: In the split-valence basis 6-31G, how many basis functions describe each inner-shell (core) orbital?

choices.why: Only the valence orbitals are split into two functions. Each core orbital gets one function.
The 6 Gaussians are combined into a single function. So each core orbital has one basis function.

choices.text: None; core orbitals are left out
choices.why: Core orbitals are included: the 6 before the hyphen counts the Gaussians in each one's function.

explanation: In N-MPG, each inner-shell orbital is one function built from N Gaussians, so in 6-31G it is one function of 6 Gaussians. Only the valence shell is split.

prompt: In a split-valence basis set such as 3-21G, how is each valence orbital represented?

choices.text: By a smaller and a larger function
By one function made of many Gaussians
choices.why: That describes a core orbital, or any orbital in a minimal basis. Split-valence sets give each valence orbital two functions.

choices.text: By two functions of the same size
choices.why: Two identical functions would add no flexibility. One is smaller and one larger, so the orbital's size can adjust.
d functions are polarization functions, not part of the split. Each valence orbital gets a smaller and a larger function.

explanation: In a split-valence set, each valence orbital is described by two functions: a smaller one built from M Gaussians and a larger one built from P. In 3-21G these are 2 and 1 Gaussians.

prompt: In 6-311G, each digit after the hyphen stands for one function used for each valence orbital. What kind of valence description is this?

choices.why: Double-ζ, as in 6-31G, has two digits after the hyphen. 6-311G has three.
A minimal basis such as STO-3G has one function per orbital and no split. 6-311G has three digits after the hyphen.
There are three digits after the hyphen, 3, 1 and 1, so three functions, not four.

explanation: The three digits 3, 1 and 1 after the hyphen mean three functions for each valence orbital, a triple-ζ valence. As with triple-ζ sets in general, accuracy improves and cost rises.

prompt: Both 3-21G and 6-31G split each valence orbital into two functions. How does 6-31G differ from 3-21G?

choices.text: More Gaussians in core and inner valence
Three functions for each valence orbital
choices.why: 6-31G has two digits after the hyphen, so two functions per valence orbital, just like 3-21G.
Neither name has an asterisk, so neither adds polarization functions.
The G in both names shows that both are Gaussian basis sets.

explanation: The core function uses 6 Gaussians in 6-31G but 3 in 3-21G, and the smaller valence function uses 3 instead of 2. The larger valence function uses 1 Gaussian in both.

prompt: In a minimum basis set, lithium gets five basis functions (1s, 2s and three added p functions) and hydrogen gets one (1s). How many basis functions does lithium hydride, LiH, have?
explanation: 5 + 1 = 6. Lithium has no p electrons, but the minimum basis still adds p-type functions to its 1s and 2s functions.

prompt: In STO-nG, each basis function is a combination of n primitive Gaussians. A neon atom has five basis functions in a minimal basis. How many primitive Gaussians does STO-6G use for neon?
explanation: 5 functions × 6 Gaussians = 30 primitive Gaussians. Each of neon's five STOs, core and valence alike, is fitted with 6 Gaussians.

prompt: A quadruple-ζ basis uses four basis functions for each atomic orbital. An oxygen atom has five atomic orbitals in a minimal basis (1s, 2s and three 2p). How many basis functions does a quadruple-ζ basis give oxygen?
explanation: 5 orbitals × 4 functions = 20 basis functions, four times the 5 of a minimal basis.

prompt: In 6-311G, each valence orbital is described by three functions built from 3, 1 and 1 primitive Gaussians. How many primitive Gaussians describe one valence orbital in all?
explanation: 3 + 1 + 1 = 5 primitive Gaussians, spread over three functions. The core orbitals each use one function of 6 Gaussians.

prompt: In 6-31G, a carbon atom carries 9 basis functions (one core function plus two for each of four valence orbitals) and a hydrogen atom carries 2 (its 1s split in two). How many basis functions does methane, CH4, have in 6-31G?
explanation: 9 + 4 × 2 = 9 + 8 = 17 basis functions. In a minimal basis methane would have only 5 + 4 = 9.

prompt: In the basis-set name 3-21G, how many primitive Gaussians describe each inner-shell (core) orbital?
explanation: The digit before the hyphen, N = 3, is the number of Gaussians for each inner-shell orbital. The 2 and 1 after the hyphen count the Gaussians in the two valence functions.
